Surah al-ʿAlaq

It is also called Surat Iqra'. There is no disagreement that it is Meccan; the disagreement concerns the number of its verses. According to the Hijazi reckoning it has twenty verses, according to the Iraqi nineteen, and according to the Shami eighteen. As for whether it was the first to be revealed or not, many scholars held that it was the first revealed, for al-Tabarani in al-Kabir, with his chain of narration, which meets the conditions of the Sahih, related from Abu Raja' al-ʿUtaridi who said: "Abu Musa al-Ash'ari used to teach us, seating us in circles, wearing two white garments. When he recited this surah, ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾

he said: 'This is the first surah that was revealed to Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).'"

Al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and they both declared it sound, related something similar from ʿAʾisha.

Many narrators related from Mujahid that he said: "The first of the Qur'an to be revealed was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾, then ﴿Nun. By the pen﴾." Al-Shaykhan related from Abu Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman who said: "I asked Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah: Which part of the Qur'an was revealed first?

He said: 'O you who are wrapped up.' I said: 'They say: Read in the name of your Lord?' He said: 'I will tell you what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) told us,'" and he went on relating the hadith, using it as evidence for what he claimed. The earlier scholars answered this with several answers that have already been mentioned. It was also said: it is al-Fatihah. Support for this was drawn from a mursal hadith whose narrators are trustworthy, related by al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il and al-Wahidi through the route of Yunus ibn Bukayr from Yunus ibn ʿUmar from his father from Abu Maysara ʿAmr ibn Shurahbil. It was answered that what it contains may be understood as a report of what was revealed after "Read" and "O you who are wrapped up," and moreover other reports are stronger in transmission. Jabir ibn Zayd affirmed decisively that the first revealed was "Read," then "Nun," then "O you who are wrapped up," then "O you who are covered," then al-Fatihah. It was also said: the first revealed was its beginning, up to what he did not know, in the Cave of Hira', and then its end was revealed after that, at what time Allah willed. This is the apparent meaning of what Imam Ahmad, al-Shaykhan, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, ʿAbd al-Razzaq and others related through the route of Ibn Shihab from ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr from ʿAʾisha in the hadith of the beginning of revelation, in which: "He (the angel) seized me and squeezed me the third time until I reached exhaustion, then he released me and said: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ ﴿created man from a clot﴾ ﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous﴾ ﴿who taught by the pen﴾ ﴿taught man what he did not know﴾." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned with it, his shoulders trembling, until she said: "Then not long after, Waraqa died, and the revelation paused."

At the end of what they related, Ibn Shihab said: Abu Salama informed me from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Ansari, who said, while speaking about the pause in revelation, in his hadith: "While I was walking, I heard a voice from the sky. I raised my gaze and there was the angel who had come to me at Hira' sitting on a chair between the sky and the earth. I was terrified of him and returned, and I said: 'Wrap me up, wrap me up.' Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ ﴿Arise and warn﴾ ﴿and your Lord, glorify﴾ ﴿and your garments, purify﴾ ﴿and uncleanness, forsake﴾. Then the revelation became intense and followed in succession."

From this it is known that the argument for the surah al-Muddaththir being the first of the Qur'an without qualification is weak, based on what was first related from the aforementioned Jabir, as is not hidden from one who examines it. We have already mentioned, at the beginning of the discussion on surah al-Muddaththir, his words there, "while speaking about the pause in revelation," and his words "then the angel who had come to me at Hira'," and his words "then the revelation became intense and followed in succession," meaning after its pause. In sum: the correct view, as some have said and which I choose, is that the beginning of this noble surah is the first of the Qur'an to be revealed without qualification. How could it not be, when the hadith of the beginning of revelation related from ʿAʾisha is among the most authentic hadiths, and in it: "The angel came to him and said: Read. He said: I said: 'I am not one who reads'..." etc. The apparent meaning is that "mā" in it is negative. Indeed al-Nawawi said it is the correct reading, and that is only conceivable if it was the first revelation, since otherwise refusal would be among the gravest sins. This agrees with what the scholars mentioned in the chapter on delaying clarification, which we will point to, God willing. In al-Kashf: the proper course is to read Jabir's words as referring to the complete surah. In Sharh Sahih Muslim: the correct view is that the first revealed was "Read," meaning absolutely, and the first revealed after the pause in revelation was "O you who are wrapped up." As for the view of those exegetes who said the first revealed was al-Fatihah, its invalidity is too clear to need mention. End.

The complete discussion on this matter is to be sought in its proper place, and God knows best. When He, glorified is He, mentioned in surah al-Tin the creation of man in the best form, He here made clear that He, the Exalted, created man from a clot. So what preceded serves as an explanation of the formal cause, and this serves as an explanation of the material cause. He, glorified is He, also mentioned here some of man's states in the Hereafter that are more detailed than what He mentioned there. He, glorified and exalted, said:

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

﴿Read﴾: that is, what is revealed to you of the Qur'an. The object is therefore omitted, by the indication of the context, as has been said. The verb is not treated as intransitive, nor is its object His saying ﴿in the name of your Lord﴾ on the grounds that the "bā'" is extra, as Abu ʿUbayda said, who claimed that the meaning is "mention your Lord." Rather it is original, its meaning being accompaniment, and it is connected to what is with it or to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause, as related from Qatada.

The meaning: ﴿Read﴾ beginning or opening ﴿in the name of your Lord﴾, that is, say "In the name of Allah" and then read. This is evident in that if one began without His name, glorified and exalted is He, one would not be complying. It has been used as evidence that the basmala is part of every surah, but there is room for discussion on this; likewise the use of it as evidence that it is not part of the Qur'an, by way of contrast, since one may say that it specifies the Qur'an intended as the object by something other than it. Some have argued that it is not Qur'an at the beginnings of surahs because it is not mentioned in the sound reports of the beginning of revelation describing how these verses were revealed; so al-Nawawi, may Allah have mercy on him, relates. Then he said: The answer of those who affirm it is that it was not revealed first, but was revealed at another time, just as the rest of the surah was. This contradicts what al-Wahidi related from ʿIkrima and al-Hasan that they both said: "The first of the Qur'an to be revealed was: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful, and the first surah was Read." It also contradicts what Ibn Jarir and others related through al-Dahhak, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The first thing Jibril, peace be upon him, said to the Prophet (ﷺ) was: O Muhammad, seek refuge, then say: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful." The view that it was the first revealed has been counted among the opinions on determining the first revealed part of the Qur'an.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti said: This view is not, in my opinion, to be counted as an independent view, for it follows necessarily from the revelation of the surah that the basmala was revealed with it; so it is the first verse revealed without qualification. But this has clear objection, as is not hidden.

It is permissible that the "bā'" is for seeking help, connected to what is with it or to an omitted element functioning as a circumstantial clause, but accompaniment is preferred for its freedom from the implication that the name of Allah is an instrument for something else. What relates to this was mentioned at the beginning of the book. Furthermore, in the command mentioned there is no imposition of what cannot be borne, whether the command indicates immediacy or not, because the Prophet (ﷺ) knew that what was revealed was Qur'an, and so he was the one charged with reciting it. There is no objection to "Read..." etc. being commanded to be recited, since he who is commanded to recite it is the one addressed by it. This is like when you say to someone: "Listen to what I say to you," for he is commanded to listen to this utterance as well. A group of the jurists of legal theory have said that this is an explanation of what was commanded in Jibril's words, "Read," mentioned in the hadith of the beginning of revelation agreed upon. Al-Amidi, in mentioning the proofs for the permissibility of delaying clarification beyond the time of address, which a group of the Hanafis and others held, said: Among the proofs is what is related: "Jibril, peace be upon him, said to the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Read﴾. He said: 'What shall I read?' He repeated it to him three times, then said to him: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾."

So the clarification of what he was first commanded, despite its generality, was delayed until after three repetitions of Jibril's command and the Prophet's question, though it was possible to clarify it at first. That is evidence for the permissibility of delay, to the end of what he said, a question and answer whose point does not concern our purpose here. It is not hidden that this being a clarification of the intended meaning in the way we have described is evident; but that it is so by taking ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ up to the end of what was revealed, or ﴿in the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ ﴿Read﴾ etc., as what al-Jalal claimed, the object of "read" repeated in Jibril's speech, is something I do not think any jurist of legal theory would hold. Likewise it being so by reading the verse according to what you heard from Abu ʿUbayda. As for building the argument on what some reports say, that Jibril came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was at Hira' with a brocade cloth on which was written: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ up to ﴿what he did not know﴾, and said to him: "Read," and he, peace be upon him, said: "I am not one who reads," and he said: "Read in the name of your Lord"—on the basis that "Read..." etc. was a clarification and a recitation by Jibril, peace be upon him, of what was on the revealed cloth, since he had no knowledge of what was in it, even though it was seen, is in the position of an unclear, unknown matter, and its state is not hidden, so consider it. Moreover, there is in al-Amidi's account, regarding the transmission of the report, what is in it, so do not be heedless.

The mention of the title of Lordship, which indicates nurture and conveyance to the fitting perfection gradually, together with its attribution to his pronoun, peace and blessings be upon him, signals his conveyance, peace be upon him, to the farthest reach of human perfections by the descent of mass-transmitted revelation.

The description of the Lord by His saying, the Exalted, ﴿who created﴾ serves to remind him, peace and blessings be upon him, of the first of the bounties flowing upon him from Him, glorified is He, together with what this contains of alerting to His power, the Exalted, to teach reading in the most gentle manner. It has been said: it is to affirm that none other than Him, the Exalted, is intended by "Lord," for the Arabs used to call idols lords, yet they did not attribute creation to them. The verb is either treated as intransitive, meaning "the One who has creation," or its object is omitted and general, meaning "the One who created everything." The first also indicates generality; so on both views the reason for singling out man for mention in His saying, the Exalted:

﴿Who created man﴾. He is the most excellent of created beings, and in him are the wonders of craftsmanship and design that are found in him. Therefore he is more indicative of the obligation of the purposeful worship that is the aim of recitation, even though the revelation (al-tanzil) is sent down to him. It is also possible that what is meant is the creation of man, but it was not mentioned first and was mentioned second deliberately, to magnify him by means of ambiguity followed by explanation. It is related from al-Zamakhshari that the appropriate reading is that what is meant is the creation of man after the command to recite the Qur'an, as an alert that He, exalted is He, created him for recitation and comprehension, just as the mention of the creation of man came after the teaching of the Qur'an at the beginning of Surat al-Rahman, for a similar reason.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from a clot﴾, that is, from congealed blood, to show the perfection of His power, exalted is He, by manifesting the clear contrast between his first and last states. He expressed it in the plural (ʿalaq) because "man" is intended as a genus, so it carries the sense of the plural. Thus He mentioned that from which he was created in the same form, so that it would agree with him, along with what this involves of observing the fawasil (verse-endings, the rhyming closings of verses). Perhaps, as has been said, the secret in singling out this stage from among all the other stages of the human natural disposition (fitrah) is that the drop of semen and the dust are more indicative of the perfection of power, since they are further removed from humanity.

In al-Bahr (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit by Abu Hayyan): He, glorified is He, did not mention the material of the origin, meaning Adam, peace be upon him, which is dust, because his creation from that was not established among the disbelievers. So He mentioned the material of the offspring and his creation from it, and left out the material of the original creation, to bring it closer to their understanding. And this, despite what is in it, does not close off the question.

It has been said: this stage was singled out as a reminder to him, upon him be prayers and peace, of what took place of the opening of the chest before prophethood and the removal of the clot from it, so that he would be fully prepared for what would come to him afterwards. It is as if it were said: He who created man from the kind of what He removed from your noble chest, so that by that He would prepare you for the like of what is being cast to you now. By this the connection of this surah with the preceding Surat al-Sharh becomes stronger, a fuller connection, especially according to the interpretation of al-Sharh as splitting open. So reflect on it.

Some people claimed that what is meant by man is Adam, peace be upon him, and that the meaning is: He created Adam from clay that clings to the hand. This is something that the hand of acceptance does not grasp. And since the creation of man was the first of the blessings poured out upon him from Him, and the most ancient of the proofs indicating His existence, mighty and majestic is He, and the perfection of His power, knowledge and wisdom, glorified is He, He described His own essence, exalted is He, with this first, so that upon him be prayers and peace would take evidence from it regarding His enabling him to recite.

Then the Majestic and Exalted repeated the command with His words, "Read" (﴿اقْرَأْ﴾), meaning: do what you have been commanded to do, as an emphasis of the obligation and a preparation for what follows from His words, "And your Lord is the Most Generous" (﴿ورَبُّكَ الأكْرَمُ﴾) and so on, for it is a resumed statement. It was intended to remove the excuse that the Prophet ﷺ had, by his words, peace be upon him, to Jibril, peace be upon him, when he said to him "Read" and he said: "I am not one who reads" («ما أنا بِقارِئٍ»).

He meant that reading is the matter of one who writes and reads, while I am unlettered. So it was said: "And your Lord," who commanded you to read, beginning and starting with His name, "the Most Generous," "who taught by the pen" (﴿الَّذِي عَلَّمَ بِالقَلَمِ﴾), that is, He taught what was taught through the medium of the pen and not by anyone else, Exalted is He. Just as He, glorified is He, taught the reader through writing with the pen, He teaches you without it. The true meaning of generosity (karam) is giving what is fitting without any purpose, so it is an attribute in which no one shares with Him, Exalted is He, in its application, so do it for emphasis. It is also permitted that "Read" here is not an emphasis of the first, but was mentioned so that what removes the excuse might be connected to it. Thus the clause "And your Lord..." and so on is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the hidden pronoun within it.

The construction ﴿عَلَّمَ الإنْسانَ ما لَمْ يَعْلَمْ﴾ is a *badal ishtimal* (a substitute that includes what it replaces) for ﴿عَلَّمَ بِالقَلَمِ﴾. That is, He taught him by means of the pen, and He taught him without it, the matters both universal and particular, both manifest and hidden, that had never occurred to his mind. The object is omitted first and then mentioned second under the heading of being unknown, which indicates the perfection of God's power and the perfection of His generosity, glory be to Him and exalted is He, and it conveys that God teaches His Prophet, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him, knowledge that the intellects cannot encompass. This is what is said in *al-Irshad*, and it is not hidden.

Some scholars held that the object of ﴿عَلَّمَ﴾ is "writing" (*al-khatt*), and they took "bil-qalam" (by the pen) as related to it. This was supported by the reading of Ibn al-Zubayr: "Alladhi 'allama al-khatta bil-qalam" (Who taught writing by the pen), where this is stated explicitly. Al-Jubba'i said: the first ﴿اقْرَأْ﴾ is a command to recite for its own sake; it is said also that it is unrestricted. The second is a command to recite for the purpose of conveying (the message); and it is said that it refers to the prayer alluded to later on. The clause ﴿ورَبُّكَ﴾ etc. may be either a circumstantial clause (*hal*) or a resumptive clause (*isti'nafiyya*). The sense, if the recitation is understood as recitation for the purpose of conveying, is in the sense of "Convey to your people."

﴿ورَبُّكَ الأكْرَمُ﴾: the One who rewards you for your deed in accordance with what His generosity requires, and who strengthens you to preserve the Qur'an so that you may convey it. The most preferred and most evident of the views is the emphatic (*ta'kid*) reading. Some scholars went far astray and claimed that "bismi" in the basmala is related to the first ﴿اقْرَأْ﴾, and "bismi rabbika" is related to the second ﴿اقْرَأْ﴾, so that the fronting (*taqdim*) would indicate the restriction of the Name of God, exalted is He, to the beginning. It was also permitted to leave "bismillah" in its well-known sense, with ﴿اقْرَأْ﴾ being a command to initiate recitation, and "bismi rabbika" related to the second ﴿اقْرَأْ﴾ for this purpose. It is not hidden that the apparent view is that "bismi rabbika" is related to what is near it, and the fronting of the verb here is more fitting, because the surah in question, according to the established view mentioned earlier, is the first surah revealed; so the recitation in it is more important given the context. It was said that even if it is granted that other surahs were revealed before it, this does not harm the fitness of fronting the verb, because the meaning, as you have heard from Qatada, is: "Recite, beginning with the Name of your Lord"; that is, say "in the Name of God," then recite. For if one begins without the basmala, one has not complied, let alone begins with something contrary to it, such as the names of idols. And if the verb were fronted, it would convey another meaning, namely that what is required at the time of recitation is that the beginning be with the Name of God, exalted is He, and not with the names of idols; and the recitation itself would not be the thing required, since it is known that the implication of fronting is that the basic act is presupposed as it is, whether as a command or as a statement, in respect of time. Whoever related the preposition to the second verb answered that the requirement of recitation in itself was derived from the first ﴿اقْرَأْ﴾, so do not be heedless.

The apparent view is that the one taught by the pen is not specified. It was said: he is every prophet who wrote. Al-Dahhak said: he is Idris, peace be upon him, and he was the first to write. Ka'b said: he is Adam, peace be upon him, and he was the first to write. They have attributed to Adam and Idris, peace be upon them, particular inscriptions in the writing of the letters of the alphabet, and it is most likely, in one's assessment, that this is not correct. God, glory be to Him and exalted is He, has incidentally drawn attention to the excellence of the knowledge of writing, because of its great benefits and the lofty ranks it attains; were it not for it, no religion would stand and no life would be well ordered. Even if there were no other proof of God's subtle wisdom and delicate governance, glory be to Him, the matter of the pen and writing would suffice. It has been said concerning it:

The saliva of deadly serpents is its saliva,
and the honey which skillful hands have gathered from the fruit.

Among what al-Zamakhshari attributed in this regard to some people, and what is said to have been intended by himself, is:

Ruqash-patterned curls like the Arqam serpents,
their steps are quick, the farthest reach swift to fall upon them.

Black of legs, their journey is not achieved
except when white reeds play with them.

They have a decisive discourse on this subject which the book cannot contain. The apparent reports indicate that writing was ancient among the nations other than the Arabs, while among them it was newer, especially among the people of the Hijaz. Many have mentioned that writing was transmitted to them from the people of al-Hira, and that they took it from the people of al-Anbar. Al-Kalbi and al-Haytham ibn Adi mentioned that the one who transmitted Arabic script from Iraq to the Hijaz was Harb ibn Umayya, who had come to al-Hira and then returned to Makkah with it. It is said that he was asked about his son Abu Sufyan: "From whom did your father take this script?" He said: "From Aslam ibn Sidra." And he said: "I asked Aslam: 'From whom did you take this script?' He said: 'From its inventor, Muramir ibn Murra.'" It was also said that Himyar had a script called *al-Musnad*, its letters separated and not joined, and it had a special status among them, so none undertook it except one who had been permitted to learn it. The kinds of writing are many. Some claimed that most of the scripts of the nations are twelve types: Arabic, Himyarite, Persian, Hebrew, Greek, Roman, Coptic, Berber, Andalusian, Indian, Chinese, and Syriac. Perhaps this, if correct, is in terms of the basic types; otherwise the branches are such that no pen could enumerate them, as is not hidden. And God, exalted is He, knows best.

Some scholars did not regard it as proper etiquette to describe anyone other than God, exalted is He, as "the Most Generous" (*al-Akram*), as many people do in their letters, writing: "To so-and-so, the Most Generous." Yet despite this, they regard it as a lowly description and find it objectionable when applied to kings and the like among the great. Sometimes they describe a Jew, a Christian, or the like with it, even though He, exalted is He, says: ﴿ورَبُّكَ الأكْرَمُ﴾. So the servant must observe proper etiquette with his Master, giving thanks for the generosity He has bestowed upon him.

﴿Kalla﴾ (indeed not / nay) is a rebuke directed at whoever among mankind disbelieves in the blessing of Allah the Exalted upon him, through his transgression, even though it is not mentioned, because the context indicates it. This is because the opening of the surah up to this section points to the great favour of Allah the Exalted upon man. So when it is said, ﴿Kalla﴾, it is a rebuke to the human being who met those noble blessings with ingratitude and transgression. Likewise is the causal clause, the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Inna al-insana la-yatgha﴾ (Verily, man does transgress), i.e., he surely oversteps the bounds in disobedience and in following the desires of the self, and waxes arrogant against his Lord, Mighty and Majestic.

Al-Kalbi said: i.e., he surely rises from one station to another in clothing, food and other things, but that is not what is meant. Some have supplied, after the saying of Allah the Exalted, ﴿what he did not know﴾, the phrase: "so that he would give thanks for those magnificent blessings, but he transgressed and disbelieved." Then ﴿Kalla﴾.

It has also been said: Kalla here means "truly" (haqqan), because there is no apparent object toward which the rebuke and deterrence are directed. Thus His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿Inna al-insana﴾ etc. is an explanation of what is intended to be affirmed, and this extends to the end of the surah. It was said that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl after a period from the revelation of the preceding verses, and this is the apparent view. And with its revelation concerning that accursed one, the intended meaning of "al-insan" is the genus (mankind).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 96, verse 7:

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿That he sees himself as self-sufficient﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi); that is: he transgresses because he sees himself as self-sufficient. This is on the basis that the clause ﴿istaghna﴾ (he sees himself as self-sufficient) is a second object of ra'a (to see), because it has the meaning of 'alima (to know). For this reason it is permissible for its subject and its object to be two pronouns referring to one thing, as in: ʿallamtanī (you taught me). They have said that this does not occur except in verbs of the heart (af'al al-qulub), and it is absent and non-existent elsewhere. A group of scholars held that ra'a in its visual sense (ra'a al-basariyya) may take the ruling of the cognitive sense (al-qalbiyya) in this respect, and they cited as an example the saying of ʿĀʾisha: "We had indeed seen ourselves with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and we had no food except the two blacks." They also recited:

"And indeed I see myself a target for the spears, sometimes from my right and sometimes in front of me."

If ra'a is taken here as visual (basariyya), then the clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), and the cause of his transgression is his seeing (himself), not the self-sufficiency itself, as His, the Exalted's, saying indicates: ﴿And if Allah were to expand provision for His servants, they would surely commit excess in the earth﴾, to signal that the basis of his transgression is his corrupt assumption according to the first view, and the mere sight of the apparent state without reflection and contemplation of its reality according to the second. On both views, the intended meaning of al-istighna' is wealth in terms of property, i.e., the opposite of the well-known poverty. It has been said: the intended meaning is that he sees himself as self-sufficient from his Lord, the Exalted, by his tribe, his wealth and his strength; but this is contrary to the apparent meaning, and the apparent meaning of what has been narrated rules it out, that "Abu Jahl said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: 'Do you claim that whoever is self-sufficient transgresses? Then make the mountains of Makkah gold and silver for us, that perhaps we may take from them and transgress, and so abandon our religion and follow your religion.' Then Jibril, peace be upon him, descended and said: 'If you wish, we will do that; then if they do not believe, we will do to them what we did to the People of the Table (ashab al-ma'ida).' So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ refrained from supplication, out of concern for them."

Qunbul, according to one of the transmissions from him, recited ﴿an ra'ahu﴾ with the omission of the alif after the hamza, which is the lam of the verb. Ibn Mujahid narrated this from him but considered it an error and said: such an omission is not permissible. In al-Bahr it is said: it is appropriate not to deem him in error, but rather to seek a justification for it. The alif has been omitted in similar cases; he said:

"Al-Ajjaj enjoined me concerning whom he enjoined me." He means: "wasiyani" (enjoined me), so he omitted the alif, which is the lam of the verb. It has also been omitted in the present tense of ra'a in their saying: "Hardship has befallen the people; if only you could see (lau tara) the people of Makkah." This is an omission that is not regular (la yantaqis). However, when the transmission is authentic, acceptance is obligatory, and the readings have come in accordance with the language of the Arabs, its regular and its irregular forms alike.

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on surah 96, verse 8:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, to your Lord is the return﴾ is a threat to the tyrant (al-taghi) and a warning to him of the consequence of tyranny (al-tughyan). It has been said that the address is to mankind (al-insan), and the shift (al-iltifat) from the third person to the second is for the intensification of the threat. It is also permissible that the address be to the master of those addressed, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The intent here is also a threat to the tyrant and a warning to him, and this is perhaps the more apparent view, considering the addresses before it. Al-Ruj'a (the return) is a verbal noun (masdar) meaning "the return," like al-busha (the good news), and the alif in it is for the feminine. The placing of the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) before its verb is for restriction (al-qasr); that is: indeed, to your Lord is the return of all by death and resurrection, not to other than Him, Glorified is He, whether independently or jointly, so you will then see the consequence of tyranny. It has been said that these verses contain idmaj (the incorporation of) an admonition against the blameworthiness of wealth, just as the first verses contain the incorporation of an admonition praising knowledge. And that suffices as an encouragement to religion and knowledge and as a deterrent from the world and wealth.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 96, verses 9–10:

And His saying, exalted is He:
Page 183
﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾ This is a mention of some of the effects of transgression (tughyan) and a threat against them. The exegetes did not differ, as Ibn 'Atiyyah said, that the servant who prays is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the one who forbids is the accursed Abu Jahl.

For Ahmad, Muslim, al-Nasa'i and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah that "Abu Jahl swore by al-Lat and al-'Uzza: 'If I see Muhammad praying, I will surely step on his neck and rub his face in the dust.' He came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was praying, intending to do this, but suddenly he was seen retreating on his heels and shielding himself with his hands. It was said to him: 'What is the matter with you?' He said: 'Between me and him there is a trench of fire, and terror, and wings.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Had he come near me, the angels would have snatched him limb from limb.' Then Allah revealed: ﴿Nay, indeed man transgresses﴾ to the end of the surah."

The saying of al-Hasan that it was Umayyah ibn Khalaf who used to forbid Salman from prayer hardly holds true, because there is no disagreement that Salman's (may Allah be pleased with him) Islam took place in Medina after the Hijrah, just as there is no disagreement that the surah is Meccan. Yes, the ruling of the verse is general, so if what is related about Umayyah occurred, its ruling would encompass him. The prayer which the verse refers to was, as Abu Hayyan related, the Zuhr prayer, and he also related that it was prayed in congregation, and that it was the first congregation established in Islam, and that with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were Abu Bakr and 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with them both). Then Abu Talib passed by with his son Ja'far, and he said to him: "O my son, join the wing of your cousin," and he departed rejoicing and composed:

Indeed 'Ali and Ja'far are my trust
in the time of the calamities of the age and its distresses.

By Allah, I will not forsake the Prophet, nor
will one who is of my lineage forsake him.

Do not forsake him, and support your cousin,
my brother from my mother, and from among them, my father.

Yet this is open to scrutiny, because prayer was made obligatory on the night of the Isra' without dispute, and Ibn Hazm claimed consensus that it was one year before the Hijrah, while Ibn Faris asserted with certainty that it was a year and three months before it, and al-Suddi said: a year and five months. The death of Abu Talib was about three years before the Hijrah, because it was three days before the death of Khadijah, or it was said five days, and her death was ten years after the mission according to the correct view. Thus Abu Talib, on this basis, did not live to see the obligation of prayer. Yes, al-Qadi 'Iyad related from al-Zuhri, and al-Nawawi and al-Qurtubi preferred, that the Isra' was five years after the mission, but objections have been raised to this, so let it be consulted.

It has been said that the prohibition (al-nahy) means prevention (al-man'), and it was expressed this way to indicate that the accursed one had no power over anything other than that. In some reports there is something whose apparent meaning is that a verbal prohibition occurred from him: Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, "He said: The Prophet (ﷺ) was praying, when Abu Jahl came and said: 'Did I not forbid you from this? Did I not forbid you from this?...' the hadith." The expression with what indicates the present/future tense is to evoke the past image because of its strangeness. It has been said that the seeing (al-ru'yah) is of the heart (qalbiyyah), and likewise in...

God's words: ﴿Have you seen [him] who, if he is upon guidance,﴾ ﴿or enjoins piety,﴾ and His, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Have you seen [him] who denies and turns away?﴾ The first object of the first verb, the relative pronoun (mawsul), and the second and third objects are omitted. The omitted object is either a pronoun referring back to it or a demonstrative pointing to it. The second object of the third verb is His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ The first two verbs are also directed toward it, and it is implied for both of them. Its omission is for brevity. A parallel to this is: "Inform me about Zayd, if you visited him"; "Inform me about him, if you asked him"; "Inform me about him, if you sought his intercession." Does not my right require this? This is not a case of tanazu' (government of a single element by two verbs), because clauses cannot be implied in this way. Rather, it is an implied meaning of the request, and omission outside of tanazu'. The answer to the conditional in both clauses is omitted, indicated by the phrase "Does he not know?", and is to be supplied as grammatical structure requires. It has been said that what indicates it is "Have you seen," understood to mean what will be mentioned shortly, if Allah the Exalted wills, and it is to be supplied likewise. The discussion of this is also similar to what has passed just now. The hidden pronouns in "was" and the verbs following it refer to the one who forbids. What is meant by "Have you seen" is "Inform me";
[Page 184]
for since seeing is a cause of knowledge, the question about it is treated as a request for information about what it relates to. The interrogative that stands in the place of the second object is the object of the request here. This treatment, as understood from the words of some of the imams, applies both to visual seeing and to seeing of the heart, and the grammarians have two opinions on this. The address in all of these, according to what a group has chosen, is to everyone who is fit to be addressed among those who have some discernment. It has been said: it is addressed to the human being, like the address in ﴿to your Lord﴾.

The tanwin on "a servant" ('abdan), according to what appears from the words of some, is for indefiniteness. Restricting the prohibition by a temporal clause indicates that the prohibition is against prayer while engaged in it. The clauses are separated for the sake of attention to the matter of censure and threat, since it indicates that each clause is intended on its own. So He, glorified is He, first censured the one who forbids for his prohibition of prayer, and threatened him for it absolutely, by His words: ﴿Have you seen the one who﴾ and so on; that is: inform me, O you who have even a little discernment, or O human being, about the one who forbids some servant of Allah the Exalted from prayer. Does he not know that Allah the Exalted sees and observes, and will therefore recompense him for that prohibition? He, glorified is He, censured him a second time for this prohibition, and threatened him for it as well, on the supposition that he is, by his own claim, upon guidance and right conduct in the very act of prohibiting, or that by means of it he enjoins piety, since prohibiting something is an order to its opposite or entails it. So He, exalted is His affair, said: ﴿Have you seen [him] who, if﴾ and so on; that is: inform me about that forbidder: does he not know that Allah observes and will recompense him, if he is upon guidance and right conduct in the very act of prohibiting, or if he is commanding piety through it, as he claims? He, majestic is His affair, censured him a third time for this and threatened him for it as well, on the supposition that in reality, and in what Allah the Exalted says, he denies the truth of prayer and turns away from it, refusing to perform it, by His words: ﴿Have you seen [him] who, if he denies﴾ and so on; that is: inform me about that forbidder: does he not know that Allah the Exalted observes his conditions, if he denies the truth of what he forbade and turns away from performing it, as we say? The summary is that He, exalted, censured and threatened for forbidding prayer without addressing the forbidder's claimed or actual condition; then He censured and threatened him, majestic and exalted, while addressing his claimed condition; then He censured and threatened him, glorified and majestic, while addressing his actual condition. This is like an escalation in censure.

The majority hold that what falls within the two conditional clauses is not restricted to what has been mentioned, since they say: if he is upon a sound path in what he forbids of the worship of Allah the Exalted, or if he is commanding right and piety in what he orders of the worship of idols, as he claims, or if he is denying the truth and turning away from the right, as we say. It has been mentioned that the second condition is a repetition of the first, since the meaning of the first is: he is not upon guidance. This is clarified by saying that introducing the conditional particle in the first is to give loose rein in form and mockery in reality, since there can be no guidance at all in forbidding the worship of Allah the Exalted and commanding the worship of idols. In the second, the mockery is for the same reason but reversed from the first, since there is no doubt that he is one who denies and turns away, so both lead to one outcome. It has been said: the seeing in the first clause is visual, so it does not need a second object; in the second and third it is of the heart. The first object is as previously stated, and the second object is taken by the first conditional clause with its answer; in the last it is "Does he not know?" and so on, referring to what was mentioned, and in what precedes it there is an omitted element which that clause indicates. The last clause is not conjoined to what precedes it, to signal that it is independent in occurrence in reality and that it brings the threat which the answer expresses. As for the clauses before it, the conditional there serves only to widen the scope, and this is the secret of stripping it of an answer and referring it to the answer of the conditional clause following it. The address in all of them is to whoever is fit for it. The tanwin on "a servant" is for magnifying him, upon him be prayer and peace, and for magnifying the prohibition and emphasizing astonishment at it. The meaning is: inform me about that forbidder, if he is upon guidance in what he forbids of the worship of Allah the Exalted, and so on as mentioned just now: does he not know that Allah sees and observes his conditions and will therefore recompense him for them, to the extent that he dared to do what he did. It has been said: "Have you seen" in the three clauses is of the seeing of the heart, the first object of the first is the relative pronoun, and its second object is the first conditional clause with its omitted answer, dispensed with by the answer of the second conditional clause, since it is known from the necessity of contrast. The second "Have you seen" is a repetition of the first, and the third "Have you seen" with its first object omitted is independently indicated by context, since it contrasts with the first, because of the contrast between the two conditions, namely His words: ﴿if he is﴾ and so on, and His words, glorified is He:
[Page 185]
﴿if he denies﴾ and so on. The bringing of the last clause without conjunction reinforces the rebuking statement and signals the truth of the condition; for this reason its answer is stated explicitly, so that it may be purely a threat. The address is as previously stated at first, and the speech is of the kind that is fair and gives loose rein. For this reason it says "a servant" and does not say "a chosen prophet." It is as if it were said: inform me, O you who have even a little discernment, about the condition of this one who forbids some servant of Allah the Exalted, let alone the chosen Prophet, from his prayer, if that forbidder is upon guidance in what he forbids of the worship of Allah the Exalted, or if he is commanding piety in what he orders of the worship of idols, as he claims; and likewise if he is in denial of the truth and turning away from the correct religion, as you say: "Does he not know?" and so on.

It has been said: "Have you seen" in the second and third clauses is a repetition of the first, and the two conditional clauses with their answers stand in place of the second object of the first. "Does he not know?" and so on is the answer of the second condition, and the answer of the first is omitted, indicated by it. He did not say: "Or if he denies" and so on, because it is not a counterpart to what precedes it, according to what has been said. The meaning is as you have heard. It has been objected to all these opinions that allowing an interrogative to come as the apodosis of a conditional without the particle fa' (fa of consequence), even though al-Zamakhshari stated it explicitly in his Kashshaf and al-Radi approved it and cited as evidence His words: ﴿Say: Have you seen, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you suddenly or openly, will any be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?﴾, is a matter for investigation, since the apparent position of al-Zamakhshari himself in al-Mufassal, and the report of others, is that fa' is obligatory when the apodosis is a performative (insha'i) clause; and even if the interrogative does not remain in its literal sense, it does not come out of the performative category as in the Kashf.

Abu Hayyan said: the occurrence of an interrogative clause as the answer of a conditional without fa' is something I know of no one who has permitted; rather they have stated the obligation of fa' in every case that calls for a request in some way, and it is not permissible to omit it except in case of necessity or poetry. al-Damamini said in his commentary on al-Tashil: making "will any be destroyed" an apodosis is problematic, since it is not joined by fa', and joining by fa' is obligatory in such a case. It has also been objected to making the conditional clause occupy the place of the second object of "Have you seen," that its second object is only an interrogative clause, as Abu Hayyan and a group stated explicitly, or an oath clause, as in al-Irshad. al-Khafaji said: making the conditional clause in the place of the object and the interrogative clause in the place of the answer of the condition, either on its literal sense, or on the basis that because both indicate that, they are treated as if they were such, since they stand in place of the object and the answer. By what has been mentioned, al-Radi and al-Damamini in their commentary on al-Tashil explicitly stated, in the chapter on the demonstrative noun, that the second object of "Have you seen" may be an interrogative clause. So what is said, that the second object of "Have you seen" cannot be an interrogative clause, contradicts what they explicitly stated to be the preferred view of Sibawayh, so it should not be paid attention to. They did not make the address in what has been mentioned to the Prophet, Allah bless him and give him peace, nor to the disbelieving forbidder, because the context requires that the forbidder and the one forbidden be excluded from the scope of the address. Al-Bahr preferred making it to the Prophet and allowed others to make it to the disbelieving forbidder. The purpose is to depict the situation under a general heading, and this, as you see, is weak.

It has been said: the two pronouns in "if he is" and "he enjoins" refer to the servant who prays, and the pronouns in "he denies," "turns away," and "knows" refer to the one who forbids. The summary of the meaning, according to al-Farra', is: Have you seen the one who forbids a servant who prays, while the one forbidden is upon guidance and enjoins piety, and the forbidder denies and turns away? How strange is this! The apparent view is that the answer of the condition is omitted here, and it is: "How strange is this!", indicated by "Have you seen," since it conveys amazement. As for the seeing in it, it has been said to be of knowledge, and its second object is omitted, similar to this answer. It has been said to be of sight, and "Does he not know?" and so on is a new independent clause confirming and reinforcing what precedes it, and the "or" is a dividing or with the meaning of "and." It has been said: the address in the second "Have you seen" is to the disbeliever and in the first to the Prophet, Allah bless him and give him peace. So He, majestic and exalted, is like a judge before whom two litigants are present, addressing one at one time and the other at another. It is as if He, glorified, said: O disbeliever, inform me: if his prayer is guidance and his call to Allah the Exalted is a command to piety, do you forbid him? And inform me, O Messenger, if the forbidder denies the truth and turns away from the correct religion, does he not know that Allah the Exalted will recompense him? This speaker remained silent about the address in the first "Have you seen," so it has been said: it is to whoever is fit for it; it has been said: it is to the human being; it has been said: it is to the Prophet, Allah bless him and give him peace, like the address in the third. His words "do you forbid him?" may be taken as an object of "Have you seen," and may be taken as the answer of the condition, or as in the preceding one. Perhaps the mention of commanding piety in the second clause is because the prohibition, as has been said, was of prayer and of commanding it, and it would have been apparent that it should be mentioned in the first clause as well, by saying: "Have you seen the one who forbids a servant when he prays, or commands piety?" But it was omitted, being sufficient by mention in the second, and it mentioned only prayer and did not reverse, because commanding piety is a verbal call, and prayer is a call by action, and action is stronger than speech. Commanding and calling are such because the one who is followed, when he does an act, is in the force of saying: do this. It has been said: what was mentioned first is not the prohibition of prayer but the prohibition during prayer, and this may be for prayer or for something else; and the general condition of prayer, since it is restricted to perfecting the worshipper's own self through worship and perfecting others through call, so his prohibition in that state is of prayer and call together; for this reason it was mentioned in the second clause. End. So do not be negligent.

The Imam also allowed that the address in all of this is to him, peace be upon him. In explaining the meaning of ﴿Have you considered, if he is﴾ and so on, he said: "Have you considered, if he were to be upon guidance and occupied himself with his own affairs? Would it not befit him, since he is a sensible man of wealth? So if he chose the sound opinion, guidance, and commanding piety, would that not be better for him than disbelief in Allah the Exalted and forbidding His service and obedience, glorified is He? It is as if the Exalted were saying: Grieve over him, how he forfeited for himself the lofty ranks and was content with the base ranks."

Isam al-Din considered this sentence a rebuke for forfeiting what benefits, and what follows it a rebuke for earning what harms. He said: The saying of the Exalted ﴿Have you seen the one﴾ and so on is a rhetorical question about the transgression of man when he sees himself as self-sufficient. "Seen" means "observed," that is: Have you observed the one who forbids a servant when he prays, and did you recognise the transgression of the self-sufficient man, and that he is not content with his disbelief but goes beyond it to obligating the servant, who was sent to prevent disbelief, to disbelieve? The saying of the Glorified: ﴿Have you considered, if he denies﴾ and so on is a rebuke to him for what he earned of deserving punishment and distance from the Lord of lords; that is: Do you know what punishment and retribution await him? The saying of the Exalted: ﴿Does he not know﴾ and so on is a threat and a severe warning after the rebuke, for earning the state of the wretched and forfeiting the state of the fortunate. End of quotation. It is as you see, so reflect on all that has preceded. And Allah the Exalted knows best His intention.

Then, although the verse was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, may the curse of Allah be upon him, whoever forbids prayer and prevents people from it shares his threat. This does not necessitate forbidding the prohibition of prayer in a usurped house or at disliked times, because what is actually forbidden is not prayer itself but its accompanying attribute. Caution has prompted some to shy away from prohibiting it absolutely.

It is narrated from the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah ennoble his face, that he saw people praying before the Eid prayer in the musalla, and he said: "I have not seen the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, do that." It was said to him, may Allah be pleased with him: "Will you not forbid them?" He said, may Allah be pleased with him: "I fear that I would enter under the threat of His saying: ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾" In another narration: "I do not like to forbid a servant when he prays, but I will inform them of what I saw from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace."

Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, also took this same course. It is narrated that Abu Yusuf said to him: "Does the one praying, when he raises his head from bowing, say: 'O Allah, forgive me'?" He said: "He says: 'Our Lord, to You is the praise,' and prostrates." He did not explicitly prohibit it. The prohibition of other kinds of worship is analogised to the prohibition of prayer, and there is no difference between the verbal prohibition (al-nahy al-qawli) and the situational prohibition (al-nahy al-hali). Among it is that a person occupies another person away from that, and many people have been afflicted with this.

﴿if he denies﴾ and so on.
