The prohibition of other kinds of worship is analogised to the prohibition of prayer, and there is no difference between the verbal prohibition (al-nahy al-qawli) and the situational prohibition (al-nahy al-hali). Among it is that a person occupies another person away from that, and many people have been afflicted with this.

God's words: ﴿Have you seen [him] who, if he is upon guidance,﴾ ﴿or enjoins piety,﴾ and His, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Have you seen [him] who denies and turns away?﴾ The first object of the first verb, the relative pronoun (mawsul), and the second and third objects are omitted. The omitted object is either a pronoun referring back to it or a demonstrative pointing to it. The second object of the third verb is His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ The first two verbs are also directed toward it, and it is implied for both of them. Its omission is for brevity. A parallel to this is: "Inform me about Zayd, if you visited him"; "Inform me about him, if you asked him"; "Inform me about him, if you sought his intercession." Does not my right require this? This is not a case of tanazu' (government of a single element by two verbs), because clauses cannot be implied in this way. Rather, it is an implied meaning of the request, and omission outside of tanazu'. The answer to the conditional in both clauses is omitted, indicated by the phrase "Does he not know?", and is to be supplied as grammatical structure requires. It has been said that what indicates it is "Have you seen," understood to mean what will be mentioned shortly, if Allah the Exalted wills, and it is to be supplied likewise. The discussion of this is also similar to what has passed just now. The hidden pronouns in "was" and the verbs following it refer to the one who forbids. What is meant by "Have you seen" is "Inform me";
[Page 184]
for since seeing is a cause of knowledge, the question about it is treated as a request for information about what it relates to. The interrogative that stands in the place of the second object is the object of the request here. This treatment, as understood from the words of some of the imams, applies both to visual seeing and to seeing of the heart, and the grammarians have two opinions on this. The address in all of these, according to what a group has chosen, is to everyone who is fit to be addressed among those who have some discernment. It has been said: it is addressed to the human being, like the address in ﴿to your Lord﴾.

The tanwin on "a servant" ('abdan), according to what appears from the words of some, is for indefiniteness. Restricting the prohibition by a temporal clause indicates that the prohibition is against prayer while engaged in it. The clauses are separated for the sake of attention to the matter of censure and threat, since it indicates that each clause is intended on its own. So He, glorified is He, first censured the one who forbids for his prohibition of prayer, and threatened him for it absolutely, by His words: ﴿Have you seen the one who﴾ and so on; that is: inform me, O you who have even a little discernment, or O human being, about the one who forbids some servant of Allah the Exalted from prayer. Does he not know that Allah the Exalted sees and observes, and will therefore recompense him for that prohibition? He, glorified is He, censured him a second time for this prohibition, and threatened him for it as well, on the supposition that he is, by his own claim, upon guidance and right conduct in the very act of prohibiting, or that by means of it he enjoins piety, since prohibiting something is an order to its opposite or entails it. So He, exalted is His affair, said: ﴿Have you seen [him] who, if﴾ and so on; that is: inform me about that forbidder: does he not know that Allah observes and will recompense him, if he is upon guidance and right conduct in the very act of prohibiting, or if he is commanding piety through it, as he claims? He, majestic is His affair, censured him a third time for this and threatened him for it as well, on the supposition that in reality, and in what Allah the Exalted says, he denies the truth of prayer and turns away from it, refusing to perform it, by His words: ﴿Have you seen [him] who, if he denies﴾ and so on; that is: inform me about that forbidder: does he not know that Allah the Exalted observes his conditions, if he denies the truth of what he forbade and turns away from performing it, as we say? The summary is that He, exalted, censured and threatened for forbidding prayer without addressing the forbidder's claimed or actual condition; then He censured and threatened him, majestic and exalted, while addressing his claimed condition; then He censured and threatened him, glorified and majestic, while addressing his actual condition. This is like an escalation in censure.

The majority hold that what falls within the two conditional clauses is not restricted to what has been mentioned, since they say: if he is upon a sound path in what he forbids of the worship of Allah the Exalted, or if he is commanding right and piety in what he orders of the worship of idols, as he claims, or if he is denying the truth and turning away from the right, as we say. It has been mentioned that the second condition is a repetition of the first, since the meaning of the first is: he is not upon guidance. This is clarified by saying that introducing the conditional particle in the first is to give loose rein in form and mockery in reality, since there can be no guidance at all in forbidding the worship of Allah the Exalted and commanding the worship of idols. In the second, the mockery is for the same reason but reversed from the first, since there is no doubt that he is one who denies and turns away, so both lead to one outcome. It has been said: the seeing in the first clause is visual, so it does not need a second object; in the second and third it is of the heart. The first object is as previously stated, and the second object is taken by the first conditional clause with its answer; in the last it is "Does he not know?" and so on, referring to what was mentioned, and in what precedes it there is an omitted element which that clause indicates. The last clause is not conjoined to what precedes it, to signal that it is independent in occurrence in reality and that it brings the threat which the answer expresses. As for the clauses before it, the conditional there serves only to widen the scope, and this is the secret of stripping it of an answer and referring it to the answer of the conditional clause following it. The address in all of them is to whoever is fit for it. The tanwin on "a servant" is for magnifying him, upon him be prayer and peace, and for magnifying the prohibition and emphasizing astonishment at it. The meaning is: inform me about that forbidder, if he is upon guidance in what he forbids of the worship of Allah the Exalted, and so on as mentioned just now: does he not know that Allah sees and observes his conditions and will therefore recompense him for them, to the extent that he dared to do what he did. It has been said: "Have you seen" in the three clauses is of the seeing of the heart, the first object of the first is the relative pronoun, and its second object is the first conditional clause with its omitted answer, dispensed with by the answer of the second conditional clause, since it is known from the necessity of contrast. The second "Have you seen" is a repetition of the first, and the third "Have you seen" with its first object omitted is independently indicated by context, since it contrasts with the first, because of the contrast between the two conditions, namely His words: ﴿if he is﴾ and so on, and His words, glorified is He:
[Page 185]
﴿if he denies﴾ and so on. The bringing of the last clause without conjunction reinforces the rebuking statement and signals the truth of the condition; for this reason its answer is stated explicitly, so that it may be purely a threat. The address is as previously stated at first, and the speech is of the kind that is fair and gives loose rein. For this reason it says "a servant" and does not say "a chosen prophet." It is as if it were said: inform me, O you who have even a little discernment, about the condition of this one who forbids some servant of Allah the Exalted, let alone the chosen Prophet, from his prayer, if that forbidder is upon guidance in what he forbids of the worship of Allah the Exalted, or if he is commanding piety in what he orders of the worship of idols, as he claims; and likewise if he is in denial of the truth and turning away from the correct religion, as you say: "Does he not know?" and so on.

It has been said: "Have you seen" in the second and third clauses is a repetition of the first, and the two conditional clauses with their answers stand in place of the second object of the first. "Does he not know?" and so on is the answer of the second condition, and the answer of the first is omitted, indicated by it. He did not say: "Or if he denies" and so on, because it is not a counterpart to what precedes it, according to what has been said. The meaning is as you have heard. It has been objected to all these opinions that allowing an interrogative to come as the apodosis of a conditional without the particle fa' (fa of consequence), even though al-Zamakhshari stated it explicitly in his Kashshaf and al-Radi approved it and cited as evidence His words: ﴿Say: Have you seen, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you suddenly or openly, will any be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?﴾, is a matter for investigation, since the apparent position of al-Zamakhshari himself in al-Mufassal, and the report of others, is that fa' is obligatory when the apodosis is a performative (insha'i) clause; and even if the interrogative does not remain in its literal sense, it does not come out of the performative category as in the Kashf.

Abu Hayyan said: the occurrence of an interrogative clause as the answer of a conditional without fa' is something I know of no one who has permitted; rather they have stated the obligation of fa' in every case that calls for a request in some way, and it is not permissible to omit it except in case of necessity or poetry. al-Damamini said in his commentary on al-Tashil: making "will any be destroyed" an apodosis is problematic, since it is not joined by fa', and joining by fa' is obligatory in such a case. It has also been objected to making the conditional clause occupy the place of the second object of "Have you seen," that its second object is only an interrogative clause, as Abu Hayyan and a group stated explicitly, or an oath clause, as in al-Irshad. al-Khafaji said: making the conditional clause in the place of the object and the interrogative clause in the place of the answer of the condition, either on its literal sense, or on the basis that because both indicate that, they are treated as if they were such, since they stand in place of the object and the answer. By what has been mentioned, al-Radi and al-Damamini in their commentary on al-Tashil explicitly stated, in the chapter on the demonstrative noun, that the second object of "Have you seen" may be an interrogative clause. So what is said, that the second object of "Have you seen" cannot be an interrogative clause, contradicts what they explicitly stated to be the preferred view of Sibawayh, so it should not be paid attention to. They did not make the address in what has been mentioned to the Prophet, Allah bless him and give him peace, nor to the disbelieving forbidder, because the context requires that the forbidder and the one forbidden be excluded from the scope of the address. Al-Bahr preferred making it to the Prophet and allowed others to make it to the disbelieving forbidder. The purpose is to depict the situation under a general heading, and this, as you see, is weak.

It has been said: the two pronouns in "if he is" and "he enjoins" refer to the servant who prays, and the pronouns in "he denies," "turns away," and "knows" refer to the one who forbids. The summary of the meaning, according to al-Farra', is: Have you seen the one who forbids a servant who prays, while the one forbidden is upon guidance and enjoins piety, and the forbidder denies and turns away? How strange is this! The apparent view is that the answer of the condition is omitted here, and it is: "How strange is this!", indicated by "Have you seen," since it conveys amazement. As for the seeing in it, it has been said to be of knowledge, and its second object is omitted, similar to this answer. It has been said to be of sight, and "Does he not know?" and so on is a new independent clause confirming and reinforcing what precedes it, and the "or" is a dividing or with the meaning of "and." It has been said: the address in the second "Have you seen" is to the disbeliever and in the first to the Prophet, Allah bless him and give him peace. So He, majestic and exalted, is like a judge before whom two litigants are present, addressing one at one time and the other at another. It is as if He, glorified, said: O disbeliever, inform me: if his prayer is guidance and his call to Allah the Exalted is a command to piety, do you forbid him? And inform me, O Messenger, if the forbidder denies the truth and turns away from the correct religion, does he not know that Allah the Exalted will recompense him? This speaker remained silent about the address in the first "Have you seen," so it has been said: it is to whoever is fit for it; it has been said: it is to the human being; it has been said: it is to the Prophet, Allah bless him and give him peace, like the address in the third. His words "do you forbid him?" may be taken as an object of "Have you seen," and may be taken as the answer of the condition, or as in the preceding one. Perhaps the mention of commanding piety in the second clause is because the prohibition, as has been said, was of prayer and of commanding it, and it would have been apparent that it should be mentioned in the first clause as well, by saying: "Have you seen the one who forbids a servant when he prays, or commands piety?" But it was omitted, being sufficient by mention in the second, and it mentioned only prayer and did not reverse, because commanding piety is a verbal call, and prayer is a call by action, and action is stronger than speech. Commanding and calling are such because the one who is followed, when he does an act, is in the force of saying: do this. It has been said: what was mentioned first is not the prohibition of prayer but the prohibition during prayer, and this may be for prayer or for something else; and the general condition of prayer, since it is restricted to perfecting the worshipper's own self through worship and perfecting others through call, so his prohibition in that state is of prayer and call together; for this reason it was mentioned in the second clause. End. So do not be negligent.

The Imam also allowed that the address in all of this is to him, peace be upon him. In explaining the meaning of ﴿Have you considered, if he is﴾ and so on, he said: "Have you considered, if he were to be upon guidance and occupied himself with his own affairs? Would it not befit him, since he is a sensible man of wealth? So if he chose the sound opinion, guidance, and commanding piety, would that not be better for him than disbelief in Allah the Exalted and forbidding His service and obedience, glorified is He? It is as if the Exalted were saying: Grieve over him, how he forfeited for himself the lofty ranks and was content with the base ranks."

Isam al-Din considered this sentence a rebuke for forfeiting what benefits, and what follows it a rebuke for earning what harms. He said: The saying of the Exalted ﴿Have you seen the one﴾ and so on is a rhetorical question about the transgression of man when he sees himself as self-sufficient. "Seen" means "observed," that is: Have you observed the one who forbids a servant when he prays, and did you recognise the transgression of the self-sufficient man, and that he is not content with his disbelief but goes beyond it to obligating the servant, who was sent to prevent disbelief, to disbelieve? The saying of the Glorified: ﴿Have you considered, if he denies﴾ and so on is a rebuke to him for what he earned of deserving punishment and distance from the Lord of lords; that is: Do you know what punishment and retribution await him? The saying of the Exalted: ﴿Does he not know﴾ and so on is a threat and a severe warning after the rebuke, for earning the state of the wretched and forfeiting the state of the fortunate. End of quotation. It is as you see, so reflect on all that has preceded. And Allah the Exalted knows best His intention.

Then, although the verse was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, may the curse of Allah be upon him, whoever forbids prayer and prevents people from it shares his threat. This does not necessitate forbidding the prohibition of prayer in a usurped house or at disliked times, because what is actually forbidden is not prayer itself but its accompanying attribute. Caution has prompted some to shy away from prohibiting it absolutely.

It is narrated from the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah ennoble his face, that he saw people praying before the Eid prayer in the musalla, and he said: "I have not seen the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, do that." It was said to him, may Allah be pleased with him: "Will you not forbid them?" He said, may Allah be pleased with him: "I fear that I would enter under the threat of His saying: ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾" In another narration: "I do not like to forbid a servant when he prays, but I will inform them of what I saw from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace."

Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, also took this same course. It is narrated that Abu Yusuf said to him: "Does the one praying, when he raises his head from bowing, say: 'O Allah, forgive me'?" He said: "He says: 'Our Lord, to You is the praise,' and prostrates." He did not explicitly prohibit it. The prohibition of other kinds of worship is analogised to the prohibition of prayer, and there is no difference between the verbal prohibition (al-nahy al-qawli) and the situational prohibition (al-nahy al-hali). Among it is that a person occupies another person away from that, and many people have been afflicted with this.

[Page 187]

﴿Nay﴾: a rebuke and a restraint for the forbidding, accursed one. The lam in His words ﴿If he does not desist﴾ is a preparatory lam (al-lam al-muwatti'ah, the lam that introduces an oath). That is, by Allah, if he does not desist from what he is doing and does not refrain, ﴿We will surely seize him by the forelock﴾, meaning we will surely take hold of his forelock and drag him by it into the Fire on the Day of Resurrection. As for al-safʿ (seizing), al-Mubarrad said: it is pulling with force. One says "safaʿa bi-nasiyat farasihi," meaning he pulled the forelock of his horse. Amr ibn Ma'dikarib said:

"A people whom, when the shouting grows loud, you see between one who bridles his colt and one who seizes it."

[Page 187 continues]

Mu'arrij said: al-safʿ means seizing, in the dialect of Quraysh. The nasiyah is the hair of the forehead, and it is also applied to the place of the hair. The alif-lam in it is for definiteness (al-ʿahd), and it is used in place of a possessive, which is the meaning of its being a substitute (ʿiwad, a replacement) for the genitive complement in such constructions. The statement is a metonymy (kinayah) for dragging him into the Fire. Abu Hayyan's claim that he expressed the whole person by the forelock is not free from problems. It was also said: the meaning is that we will drag him on his face in this world, on the Day of Badr, and in this there is good news that Allah, exalted is He, will enable the Muslims to take hold of his forelock so that they drag him, if he does not desist. And indeed He, mighty and majestic, did so. It has been narrated that when Surat al-Rahman was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Who will recite it to the chiefs of Quraysh?" Ibn Mas'ud stood up and said: "I, O Messenger of Allah." He did not permit him, because of his weakness and small body, until he said it three times, and each time Ibn Mas'ud said: "I, O Messenger of Allah." So he (ﷺ) permitted him. He came to them while they were gathered around the Ka'bah, and he began to recite. Abu Jahl stood up, slapped him, split his ear and made it bleed. He returned with his eyes shedding tears. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) descended laughing, and the Prophet (ﷺ) spoke to him about that. He (peace be upon him) said: "You will know." When the Day of Badr came, he (peace be upon him) said: "Search for Abu Jahl among the dead." Ibn Mas'ud saw him thrown down and gasping, so he climbed onto his chest. He opened his eye and recognized him, and said: "You have climbed a difficult height, O little shepherd of the goats." Ibn Mas'ud said: "Islam rises and is not risen above." He worked at cutting off his head, and the accursed one said: "Here, cut it with my sword." He cut it off but could not lift it, so he split his ear, put a cord through it, and kept dragging it until he brought it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then Jibril (peace be upon him) came laughing and said: "O Messenger of Allah, an ear for an ear, and the head is extra." It seems that the specific mention of the forelock is because the accursed one was very concerned with grooming and perfuming it, or because seizing by it was the utmost humiliation among the Arabs, since it happens only with complete control and dominance, and because their custom with beasts was that. Mahbub and Harun, both from Abu 'Amr, read "la-nasfaʿanna" with the heavy nun. Ibn Mas'ud read "la-asfaʿanna" in the same way, with the verb attributed to the first-person singular speaker alone. In the reading of the majority, the light nun was written as an alif, taking into account the state of pausing, for it is paused upon with an alif, likening it to tanwin. The rule of writing is based on the state of pausing and beginning. Among examples of this is his saying:

"And whatever you wish from him, Fazarah will prevent it."

And his saying: "The ignorant one thinks it, while he does not know."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 96, verse 16:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a forelock (nasiyah)﴾ is a substitution (badal) from "the forelock" (al-nasiyah), and its substitution from a definite noun is permissible although it is indefinite (nakirah), because it has been qualified by His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿lying, sinning﴾, so it stands alone in conveying meaning. The Basrans have mentioned that the substitution of an indefinite noun from a definite one requires only that it convey meaning, and no more. The position of the Kufans is that it may be substituted from it on two conditions: the unity of the wording and the qualification of the indefinite noun. The outward meaning covers every forelock of which this is the description, and this is achievable according to all the schools.

The qualifying of the forelock with what has been mentioned, although it is a description of its owner, is for emphasis (mubalaghah), since it indicates his being described with lying and sinning by way of priority (bi-tariq al-awla). It conveys that, because of the intensity of his lying and sinning, every part of his parts seems to lie and sin. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and their tongues describe the lie﴾, and the saying of people: "Her face describes beauty." So the attribution is metaphorical (majazi), from attributing what belongs to the whole to a part.

Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi Ablah and Zayd ibn Ali read: "a forelock lying, sinning," with all three in the accusative (nasb) by way of vituperation (al-shatm), and al-Kisa'i, in one narration, read them in the nominative (raf'), meaning: "it is a forelock," etc.

﴿Then let him call his council.﴾ Al-nadi (the gathering place where people meet) is the assembly in which the people gather for conversation, and its plural is andiyah. The phrase is understood with an omitted noun (taqdir al-mudaf, supplying the implied word): that is, "let him call the people of his council." Alternatively, the attribution is figurative (majaz), or the name of the place is applied to those who occupy it. Similar usage occurs for this kind of assembly, as Jarir or Dhu al-Rummah said:

Theirs is an assembly, of tawny-moustached men, humbled and equal, its free men and its slaves alike.

And Zuhayr said:

Among them are dignified stations whose faces are fine, and gatherings frequented by word and deed.

This refers to what is authentically related: that Abu Jahl passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was praying and said, "Did I not forbid you?" And he (ﷺ) spoke harshly to him. He said, "Are you threatening me? I am the one with the largest assembly in the valley."

The matter is as stated in al-Bahr: it is for ta'jiz (a challenge to demonstrate incapacity) and to indicate that he has no power over anything.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 96, verse 18:

Page 188
﴿We shall call the guardians of Hell﴾: that is, the angels of punishment, so that they may drag him into the Fire. The word (zabaniyah) originally refers to the police, i.e., the helpers of the rulers. Scholars differed about it. It was said: it is a plural with no singular from its own root, like ʿabadid. Abu ʿUbayda said: its singular is zibniyah, with a kasra and then a sukun, like ʿifriyah. Al-Kisa'i said: its singular is zibnā, with a kasra, as if it were ascribed to al-zabn, with a fatha, which means pushing; then it was altered for the sake of the relative form, and its first letter was given a kasra, like insiyy. The original plural is zabānīy, and it was said: zabāniyah, by deleting one of its two yas and replacing it with a ta'. ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar and al-Akhfash said: its singular is zābin. The Arabs sometimes apply this name to one whose violence is great even if he is not among the helpers of the rulers, and from this is the saying of the poet:

"Generous at the farthest reaches, spearmen in battle, mighty guardians, great of intellect."

The angels of punishment were named thus because they push those they punish into the Fire. This calling is in this world, based on what is reported: that if he had called his assembly, the zabaniyah would have seized him there and then in plain sight. Apparently, ﴿sanad'u﴾ is in the nominative because it is free of any governing or jussive particle, and it was written in the codices without a waw, following the written form to the pronunciation; for the waw is omitted in pronunciation because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, or to match ﴿fal-yad'u﴾. It was also said that it is jussive as a response to the imperative, but this is open to question.

Ibn Abi ʿAbla read: «sayu'da'u al-zabaniyatu» in the passive voice, with al-zabaniyatu in the nominative.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 96, verse 19:

﴿Kalla﴾ (No!): a rebuke to that accursed one, following a rebuke and a deterrent already given to him.

﴿Do not obey him﴾: that is, persist in what you are upon of opposing him.

﴿And prostrate﴾ and be constant in your prostration, paying no heed to him. It is either on its literal meaning, or a metaphor for prayer (salah).

﴿And draw near﴾: and get closer to your Lord by means of that.

In Sahih Muslim and others, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, raised (to the Prophet): "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating, so increase your supplication (du'a)."

Also in the Sahih and others, from the hadith of Thawban, raised: "Upon you is abundant prostration, for you do not prostrate to Allah Most High a single prostration except that Allah Most High raises you by it a degree and removes from you by it a sin."

On the basis of these reports and similar ones, a number of scholars held that prostration is the most excellent of the pillars (arkan) of prayer. It is strange that al-'Izz ibn 'Abd al-Salam, one of the great imams of the Shafi'is, held that supplication is obligatory in it.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit): it is established in the two Sahihs that "the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated in: ﴿When the sky is split open﴾" and in this surah, which is among the obligatory prostrations (al-'aza'im) according to 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face. Malik used to prostrate in it for his own personal practice. And Allah Most High is the Granter of success.
